claim: Angptl2 overexpression is sufficient to expand definitive HSPCs in zebrafish embryos.
source: Overexpression of zangptl2 is sufficient to increase zebrafish definitive hematopoiesis in vivo, recapitulating the initial finding that ANGPTL2 can expand HSPCs ex vivo (Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript describes experiments showing increased cmyb- and runx1-positive HSPCs in heatshocked Tg(hsp70:zangptl2) embryos compared to controls, as shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Heatshocked Tg(hsp70:zangptl2) embryos have increased cmyb- and runx1-positive HSPCs in the AGM at 36hpf.
source: We observed significantly higher number of cmyb- and runx1-positive HSPCs in heatshocked Tg embryos compared to their non-heatshocked or non-Tg siblings by whole mount in situ hybridization (WISH) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct observation from WISH experiments shown in Figure 1A demonstrating increased HSPC markers.

claim: Heatshocked Tg(hsp70:zangptl2) embryos have increased cmyb- and runx1-positive HSPCs in the CHT and pronephros.
source: Increased cmyb- and runx1-positive HSPCs were also found in the caudal hematopoietic tissue (or CHT, akin to mammalian fetal liver) and the pronephros, which matures into the kidney marrow, the mammalian bone marrow equivalent (Figure 1A).
evidence: WISH data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating increased HSPC markers in multiple hematopoietic tissues.

claim: Heatshocked Tg(hsp70:zangptl2) embryos have increased rag1-positive differentiated thymic T-cells.
source: Rag1-positive differentiated thymic T-cells that derive from definitive HSPCs were increased in heatshocked Tg siblings (Figure 1A).
evidence: WISH data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating increased rag1 expression in thymus.

claim: Angptl1 and 2 are required for definitive hematopoiesis in zebrafish.
source: We next performed anti-sense knockdown experiments using previously established morpholinos (MOs) (Kubota et al., 2005) and found that while single zangptl1-MO or angptl2-MO can decrease cmyb-positive HSPCs in the AGM (data not shown), knocking down both zangptls (angptls-MO) led to a near complete absence of cmyb- and runx1-positive AGM HSPCs at 36hpf (Figure 1B), indicating that zangptl1 and 2 are required for definitive HSPCs formation.
evidence: Morpholino knockdown experiments showing loss of HSPC markers in angptls-MO morphants as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Angptls-MO morphants have decreased cmyb- and runx1-positive HSPCs in the AGM at 36hpf.
source: knocking down both zangptls (angptls-MO) led to a near complete absence of cmyb- and runx1-positive AGM HSPCs at 36hpf (Figure 1B)
evidence: WISH data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating loss of HSPC markers in morphants.

claim: Angptls-MO morphants have severe disruption to vascular development with loss of kdrl-positive ISVs.
source: We found that angiogenic sprouting of kdrl-positive intersegmental vessels (ISVs) in control-MO injected (data not shown) or uninjected siblings was absent in angptls-MO morphants (Figure 1C).
evidence: WISH data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating loss of ISV formation in morphants.

claim: Angptls-MO morphants have loss of arterial efnb2a in the DA.
source: Axial vessel specification was also severely disrupted with decreased arterial efnb2a in the DA and ectopic expression of venous flt4, also in the DA, normally restricted to the posterior cardinal vein (PCV) by 28hpf (Figure 1C).
evidence: WISH data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating loss of arterial marker expression.

claim: Angptls-MO morphants have ectopic expression of venous flt4 in the DA.
source: Axial vessel specification was also severely disrupted with decreased arterial efnb2a in the DA and ectopic expression of venous flt4, also in the DA, normally restricted to the posterior cardinal vein (PCV) by 28hpf (Figure 1C).
evidence: WISH data shown in Figure 1C demonstrating ectopic venous marker expression in the DA.

claim: Zangptls regulation of definitive HSPC development may occur through early specification of hemogenic endothelium.
source: These results suggest that zangptls regulation of definitive HSPC development may occur through an early specification of a patent and functional hemogenic endothelium.
evidence: Inference based on the observed vascular defects in angptls-MO morphants occurring before HSPC formation.

claim: Zangptls1 and 2 are dispensable for primitive hematopoiesis.
source: Furthermore, gata1-positive primitive erythrocytes (Detrich et al., 1995) also appeared to be unchanged in the posterior LPM or intermediate cell mass at 24hpf (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that zangptls1 and 2 are dispensable for primitive hematopoiesis.
evidence: WISH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 demonstrating normal primitive erythrocyte formation in morphants.

claim: The angptls-MO morphant phenotypes closely resemble that of the notch mutant mib.
source: The angptls-MO morphant phenotypes closely resembled that of the notch mutant, mib (Lawson et al., 2001; Itoh et al., 2003; Burns et al., 2005), which also exhibited defective definitive hematopoiesis and vascular specification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Comparison of phenotypes between angptls-MO morphants and mib mutants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mib encodes for the highly conserved E3 ubiquitin ligase important for endocytic processing of notch ligands.
source: Mib encodes for the highly conserved E3 ubiquitin ligase important for endocytic processing of notch ligands (Itoh et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Angptls-MO morphants have reduced notch reporter eGFP expression.
source: Seen in Figure 2A, angptls-MO morphants had reduced eGFP expression, suggesting that zangptls are required for notch signaling.
evidence: Data from notch reporter transgenic line shown in Figure 2A demonstrating reduced notch activity in morphants.

claim: Zangptls are required for notch signaling.
source: angptls-MO morphants had reduced eGFP expression, suggesting that zangptls are required for notch signaling.
evidence: Inference based on reduced notch reporter activity in angptls-MO morphants.

claim: Overexpression of constitutively active notch can rescue angptls-MO morphants.
source: We observed that angptls-MO injected into heatshock-inducible double Tg, Tg(hsp70:Gal4;UAS:NICD) (Scheer et al., 2001; Burns et al., 2005) restored cmyb- and runx1-positive HSPCs (Figure 2B and data not shown).
evidence: Genetic rescue experiment shown in Figure 2B demonstrating restoration of HSPC markers.

claim: Overexpression of zangptl2 can rescue mib embryos.
source: Surprisingly, mib embryos, normally devoid of HSPCs, crossed to Tg(hsp70:zangptl2) also rescued cmyb- and runx1-positive HSPCs (Figure 2C and data not shown) at 36hpf upon heatshock.
evidence: Genetic rescue experiment shown in Figure 2C demonstrating restoration of HSPC markers in mib mutants.

claim: Zangptl signaling is downstream of mib but upstream of notch activation/NICD formation during zebrafish definitive hematopoiesis.
source: Together, these genetic relationships between zangptls and notch place zangptl signaling downstream of mib but upstream of notch activation/NICD formation during zebrafish definitive hematopoiesis.
evidence: Inference based on the genetic rescue experiments showing NICD can rescue angptls-MO and zangptl2 can rescue mib.

claim: NOTCH can exert cell autonomous effects on hemogenic endothelial cells destined to become HSPC.
source: These results highly suggest that NOTCH can exert a cell autonomous effect on hemogenic endothelial cells destined to become HSPC.
evidence: Inference based on time-lapse imaging data showing increased AGM budding events in NICD-expressing hemogenic endothelial cells.

claim: There are significantly more AGM budding events in embryos injected with constitutively active NOTCH compared to control.
source: In contrast, there was significantly more AGM budding events in embryos injected with constitutively active NOTCH (Video 1) (ranges for eGFP: 0–2; NICD: 0–6), all of which are depicted in the Figure 3C graph.
evidence: Time-lapse imaging data quantified in Figure 3C showing increased budding events.

claim: NOTCH can exert cell autonomous effects on HSPCs.
source: These results are tabulated in Figure 3D and strongly indicated that NOTCH can exert cell autonomous effects on HSPCs.
evidence: Data from CHT imaging experiments shown in Figure 3D demonstrating increased double positive HSPCs with NOTCH expression.

claim: There are significantly higher numbers of double positive HSPCs in which NOTCH is constitutively expressed compared to control.
source: Shown in Figure 3B, we can readily observe significantly higher number of double positive HSPCs in which NOTCH is constitutively expressed compared to the control eGFP transgene injected siblings.
evidence: Imaging data shown in Figure 3B and quantified in Figure 3D.

claim: MYC is a direct NOTCH target in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL).
source: The MYC proto-oncogene has been previously shown to be a direct NOTCH target in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) (Palomero et al., 2006; Weng et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Myc is critical in the regulation of hematopoietic/vascular development.
source: Moreover, Myc is also critical in the regulation of hematopoietic/vascular development (Wilson et al., 2004; Laurenti et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Conditional cMyc knockout in hematopoietic lineages resulted in severe cytopenia at E11.5 and lethality at E12.5 in mice.
source: Conditional cMyc knockout in hematopoietic lineages resulted in severe cytopenia at E11.5 and lethality at E12.5 in mice (He et al., 2008)
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Myc-deficient HSPCs are functionally defective and unable to engraft in recipient mice.
source: Myc-deficient HSPCs are functionally defective, unable to engraft in recipient mice (Wilson et al., 2004).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Myc morpholino knockdown results in significant reduction in cmyb-positive HSPCs in the AGM.
source: To first establish the role of myc during zebrafish definitive hematopoiesis, we performed morpholino knockdown of myc and observed a significant reduction in cmyb-positive HSPCs in the AGM (Figure 4A), suggesting its requirement.
evidence: Morpholino knockdown data shown in Figure 4A demonstrating loss of HSPC markers.

claim: Myc is required for zebrafish definitive hematopoiesis.
source: we performed morpholino knockdown of myc and observed a significant reduction in cmyb-positive HSPCs in the AGM (Figure 4A), suggesting its requirement.
evidence: Inference based on loss of HSPCs upon myc knockdown.

claim: Overexpression of myc in mib embryos partially restores cmyb-positive HSPCs in the AGM.
source: Next, to determine whether myc is downstream of notch during this process, we overexpressed myc in mib embryos and found partially restored cmyb-positive HSPCs in the AGM (Figure 4B).
evidence: Genetic rescue experiment shown in Figure 4B demonstrating restoration of HSPC markers.

claim: Myc is downstream of notch during zebrafish definitive hematopoiesis.
source: to determine whether myc is downstream of notch during this process, we overexpressed myc in mib embryos and found partially restored cmyb-positive HSPCs in the AGM (Figure 4B).
evidence: Inference based on genetic rescue of mib by myc overexpression.

claim: Overexpression of myc in angptls-MO morphants restores cmyb-positive HSPCs in the AGM.
source: We found similar restoration of cmyb-positive HSPCs in the AGM (Figure 4C), thereby implying that myc maybe one of the underlying effectors downstream of zangptl signaling.
evidence: Genetic rescue experiment shown in Figure 4C demonstrating restoration of HSPC markers.

claim: Myc may be one of the underlying effectors downstream of zangptl signaling.
source: We found similar restoration of cmyb-positive HSPCs in the AGM (Figure 4C), thereby implying that myc maybe one of the underlying effectors downstream of zangptl signaling.
evidence: Inference based on genetic rescue of angptls-MO by myc overexpression.

claim: Angptls may exert their effects through notch signaling to converge upon myc during zebrafish definitive hematopoiesis.
source: Together, these results further strengthened our hypothesis that angptls may exert their effects through notch signaling to converge upon myc during zebrafish definitive hematopoiesis.
evidence: Inference based on the genetic rescue experiments showing myc can rescue both mib and angptls-MO.

claim: More than 3700 genes were differentially regulated with significant q value <0.05 in ANGPTL2-stimulated human CD34+ cells.
source: More than 3700 genes were differentially regulated with significant q value <0.05 (False Discovery Rate (FDR), Benjamini-Hochberg).
evidence: Microarray analysis of ANGPTL2-stimulated CD34+ cells.

claim: 284 gene sets showed highly significant positive enrichment score with FDR<0.05 in GSEA analysis of ANGPTL2-stimulated CD34+ cells.
source: 284 gene sets showed a highly significant positive enrichment score (ES) with FDR<0.05, indicating that these sets contained genes that positively correlated with our expression phenotype, that is, upregulated in ANGPTL2-treated cells (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: GSEA analysis of microarray data from ANGPTL2-stimulated cells.

claim: The strongest correlation in GSEA analysis was found with gene sets relating to MYC signaling.
source: Despite a wide range of disease state responses or experimental parameters represented in these 284 gene sets, the strongest correlation was found with those relating to MYC signaling, an example of which is shown in Figure 4D.
evidence: GSEA analysis results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: MYC was predicted to be one of the top upstream regulators in an active state by IPA analysis of ANGPTL2 signature.
source: In concordance with the GSEA analysis, the ANGPTL2 signature was analyzed using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA), and MYC was again predicted to be one of the top upstream regulators in an active state (p-value of 2.89E-16).
evidence: IPA analysis of microarray data from ANGPTL2-stimulated cells.

claim: NOTCH ChIP-seq in ANGPTL2-stimulated human CD34+ cells shows enrichment for ETS, RUNX1, and ZNF143 motifs.
source: Similar to the previously published ChIP-seq data (Wang et al., 2011), we found enrichment for ETS, RUNX1, and ZNF143 motifs, the latter containing an embedded consensus sequence for CSL/RBPjκ (indicated by the red box in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), in the sites bound by NOTCH.
evidence: ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GREAT analysis revealed that significantly more regions in NOTCH ChIP-seq data set fall within the regulatory domains of MYC target genes.
source: GREAT (Genomic Regions Enrichment of Annotations Tool) analysis revealed in some instances, that significantly more regions in our NOTCH ChIP-seq data set fall within the regulatory domains of MYC target genes or genes that are involved in the regulation of MYC targets (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: GREAT analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IPA network analysis of NOTCH ChIP-seq revealed MYC-related genes forming the second highest ranking network.
source: Further pathway analyses using IPA revealed ​MYC-related genes forming the second highest ranking network as well as placing ​MYC as a significant upstream regulator in an active state (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: IPA analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: GSEA analysis comparing ANGPTL2 microarray signature to NOTCH ChIP-bound MYC targets showed strong and significant enrichment.
source: GSEA analysis comparing the ANGPTL2 microarray signature to the NOTCH ChIP-bound ​MYC targets showed a strong and significant enrichment (Figure 4E)
evidence: GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4E comparing microarray and ChIP-seq data.

claim: The gene expression of MYC targets identified from ANGPTL2 microarray overlapped significantly with those bound by NOTCH.
source: GSEA analysis comparing the ANGPTL2 microarray signature to the NOTCH ChIP-bound ​MYC targets showed a strong and significant enrichment (Figure 4E), suggesting that the gene expression of ​MYC targets identified from the ANGPTL2 microarray overlapped significantly with those bound by NOTCH.
evidence: Inference based on GSEA analysis results.

claim: ANGPTL2 signaling may affect NOTCH activation.
source: Together with our genetic data and the fact that these informatics analyses revealed converging signaling on ​MYC activation by ANGPTL2 and NOTCH points to the likelihood that ANGPTL2 signaling may affect NOTCH activation.
evidence: Inference based on convergence of ANGPTL2 and NOTCH signaling on MYC from multiple analyses.

claim: ANGPTL2 stimulation of human CD34+ cells results in rapid increase in NOTCH receptor cleavage generating NICD.
source: To examine whether ANGPTLs have direct effects on NOTCH, we stimulated human CD34+ progenitor cells with ANGPTL2 and observed a rapid increase in NOTCH receptor cleavage, generating the product NICD without affecting total levels of full-length NOTCH receptor (Figure 5A).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 5A demonstrating increased NICD upon ANGPTL2 stimulation.

claim: ANGPTL2 stimulation does not affect total levels of full-length NOTCH receptor.
source: we stimulated human CD34+ progenitor cells with ANGPTL2 and observed a rapid increase in NOTCH receptor cleavage, generating the product NICD without affecting total levels of full-length NOTCH receptor (Figure 5A).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 5A showing unchanged full-length NOTCH levels.

claim: ANGPTL2 treatment significantly increases HES1-luc luciferase activity.
source: First, to assess transcriptional activity of HES1, we treated cells that were transfected with the NOTCH-responsive luciferase plasmid, HES1-luc, and saw a significant increase in luciferase activity upon ANGPTL2 stimulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Luciferase assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ANGPTL2 stimulation significantly increases HES1 mRNA levels.
source: Furthermore, we found significant increase in HES1 mRNA level by qPCR during ANGPTL2-stimulation time course (Figure 5B blue bars).
evidence: qPCR data shown in Figure 5B demonstrating increased HES1 mRNA.

claim: DAPT pretreatment suppresses ANGPTL2-induced increases in HES1 mRNA.
source: Pretreating these cells with DAPT was able to suppress these increases (Figure 5B red bars), implying that this is NOTCH-dependent.
evidence: qPCR data shown in Figure 5B demonstrating DAPT blocks ANGPTL2-induced HES1 increase.

claim: ANGPTL2-induced HES1 increase is NOTCH-dependent.
source: Pretreating these cells with DAPT was able to suppress these increases (Figure 5B red bars), implying that this is NOTCH-dependent.
evidence: Inference based on DAPT blocking ANGPTL2-induced HES1 increase.

claim: ANGPTL2 treatment significantly increases RUNX1 and cMYC mRNA levels.
source: Similarly, we also detected significant increases in RUNX1 and cMYC mRNA upon ANGPTL2 treatment that are again, NOTCH dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ANGPTL2-induced increases in RUNX1 and cMYC are NOTCH dependent.
source: Similarly, we also detected significant increases in RUNX1 and cMYC mRNA upon ANGPTL2 treatment that are again, NOTCH dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inference based on DAPT blocking ANGPTL2-induced increases as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ANGPTL2 can rapidly activate NOTCH as a result of induced NOTCH receptor cleavage to initiate downstream transcription of NOTCH target genes.
source: These results indicate that ANGPTL2 can rapidly activate NOTCH as a result of induced NOTCH receptor cleavage to initiate downstream transcription of the NOTCH target genes.
evidence: Inference based on Western blot, luciferase, and qPCR data showing ANGPTL2 induces NOTCH cleavage and target gene expression.

claim: ANGPTL2 stimulates an increase in NICD in human endothelial cells.
source: As observed in Figure 5C, ANGPTL2 stimulated an increase in NICD in endothelial cells (as in CD34+ cells, Figure 5A) in vehicle (DMSO)-treated cells and this increase was blocked by DAPT.
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: DAPT blocks ANGPTL2-induced NICD increase in human endothelial cells.
source: ANGPTL2 stimulated an increase in NICD in endothelial cells (as in CD34+ cells, Figure 5A) in vehicle (DMSO)-treated cells and this increase was blocked by DAPT.
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Blocking S2 cleavage with TAPI-2 or SB-3CT inhibits NEXT and NICD formation.
source: Blocking upstream of S3 at S2 using two different inhibitors of S2 cleavage (TAPI-2, a broad spectrum ADAM and TACE inhibitor; and SB-3CT, a non-competitive inhibitor for TACE) results in inhibiting NEXT and NICD formation.
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 5C demonstrating S2 inhibitors block NEXT and NICD formation.

claim: ANGPTL2 stimulates the generation of NEXT fragment.
source: In control DMSO-treated cells, ANGPTL2 also stimulated the generation of NEXT fragment and this was further enhanced by treatment with DAPT
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ANGPTL2 may regulate NOTCH activation via S2 cleavage.
source: In control DMSO-treated cells, ANGPTL2 also stimulated the generation of NEXT fragment and this was further enhanced by treatment with DAPT, thus establishing that ANGPTL2 may regulate NOTCH activation via S2 cleavage.
evidence: Inference based on Western blot data showing ANGPTL2 induces NEXT formation which is enhanced by DAPT.

claim: The rise in NICD levels induced by ANGPTL2 is a result of NOTCH receptor cleavage as opposed to interference with NICD degradation.
source: We can conclude from this study that the rise in NICD levels induced by ANGPTL2 is a result of NOTCH receptor cleavage as opposed to interference with NICD degradation.
evidence: Inference based on NICD degradation experiment shown in Figure 5D where DAPT post-treatment reduces NICD levels.

claim: LILRB2 was identified to be the ANGPTLs receptor.
source: The human leukocyte immunoglobulin (Ig)-like receptor B2 (LILRB2) was identified to be the ANGPTLs receptor (Zheng et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to published literature.

claim: LILRB2 contains 4 Ig domains in its extracellular domain, a transmembrane domain, and 3 ITIMs in its intracellular domain.
source: Typical of the Ig superfamily, of which includes more than 850 members, LILRB2 contains 4 Ig domains in its extracellular domain (ECD), a transmembrane domain (TM), and 3 immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs (ITIMs) in its intracellular domain (ICD).
evidence: Description of LILRB2 structure based on established knowledge.

claim: LILRB2 is bound to NOTCH in transfected HEK293T cells.
source: Shown in Figure 6A, LILRB2 is bound to NOTCH and this interaction is increased upon ANGPTL2 stimulation.
evidence: Co-IP data shown in Figure 6A demonstrating LILRB2-NOTCH interaction.

claim: LILRB2-NOTCH interaction is increased upon ANGPTL2 stimulation in transfected HEK293T cells.
source: Shown in Figure 6A, LILRB2 is bound to NOTCH and this interaction is increased upon ANGPTL2 stimulation.
evidence: Co-IP data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Endogenous LILRB2 and NOTCH interact in human CD34+ cells.
source: To assess endogenous interaction between LILRB2 and NOTCH, we performed co-IPs in human CD34+ cells and observed similarly (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Co-IP data shown in Figure 6B,C demonstrating endogenous interaction.

claim: NOTCH1 interaction with LILRB2 was only observed with full-length LILRB2 or LILRB2-ECD.
source: We found that only the full-length or LILRB2 ECD can interact with NOTCH suggesting that this interaction occurs extracellularly (Figure 6D).
evidence: Co-IP data shown in Figure 6D with LILRB2 truncation mutants.

claim: LILRB2-NOTCH interaction occurs extracellularly.
source: We found that only the full-length or LILRB2 ECD can interact with NOTCH suggesting that this interaction occurs extracellularly (Figure 6D).
evidence: Inference based on co-IP data showing only ECD-containing LILRB2 interacts with NOTCH.

claim: LILRB2 and NOTCH interaction likely occurs in cis within the same cells.
source: We could not detect any interaction after replating (right lanes) while still being able to detect LILRB2 ECD interaction with NOTCH in double transfections (middle lanes), thus suggesting that the LILRB2 and NOTCH interaction likely occur in cis, that is, within the same cells extracellularly (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Replating experiment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Stable knockdown of LILRB2 results in decreased interaction between LILRB2 and NOTCH.
source: Furthermore, the interaction between LILRB2 and NOTCH receptors also decreased in sh-LILRB2 cells (Figure 6E, first blot).
evidence: Co-IP data shown in Figure 6E with LILRB2 knockdown cells.

claim: Stable knockdown of LILRB2 abolishes ANGPTL2-mediated NOTCH cleavage.
source: we saw that in contrast to the control scrambled shRNA transduced cells (sh-CT), which still retained the ANGPTL2-mediated NOTCH cleavage, sh-LILRB2 transduced cells had lost this response with no ANGPTL2-induced NICD formation (Figure 6E, third blot).
evidence: Western blot data shown in Figure 6E demonstrating loss of ANGPTL2-induced NICD in LILRB2 knockdown cells.

claim: ANGPTL2-induced NOTCH activation may occur through ligand-regulated recruitment of LILRB2 to NOTCH into the same microdomain.
source: Together, these studies demonstrate that ANGPTL2-induced NOTCH activation may occur through a ligand-regulated recruitment of LILRB2 to NOTCH into the same microdomain.
evidence: Inference based on co-IP and knockdown data showing ANGPTL2 increases LILRB2-NOTCH interaction and LILRB2 is required for ANGPTL2-induced NOTCH cleavage.

claim: Notch is indispensable during the developmental specification of HSPCs.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that notch is indispensable during the developmental specification of HSPCs (Burns et al., 2005; Clements et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Zangptl1 and 2 play an essential role during developmental hematopoiesis.
source: In our present study, we defined the essential role of zangptl1 and 2 during developmental hematopoiesis (Figure 1), likely through regulation of notch signaling in the hemogenic endothelium.
evidence: Summary statement based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: This is the first time zangptls has been shown to activate notch.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first time zangptls has been shown to activate notch.
evidence: Statement of novelty based on literature knowledge.

claim: The current model for notch specification of HSPCs during development has mostly been suggested to be cell-autonomous.
source: The current model for notch specification of HSPCs during development has mostly been suggested to be a cell-autonomous one (Hadland et al., 2004; Burns et al., 2005; Robert-Moreno et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Live imaging data from transient Tg(drl:eGFP;kdrl:NICD)-injected embryos shows significantly more budding HSPCs in the AGM.
source: Our live imaging data from transient Tg(drl:eGFP;kdrl:NICD)-injected embryos resulting in significantly more budding HSPCs in the AGM of DA corroborate with this.
evidence: Reference to live imaging data presented earlier in the manuscript.

claim: Somite-derived notch signaling during HSPC specification occurs much earlier than previously thought.
source: More recently, studies have revealed an additional and separate role for somite-derived notch signaling during HSPC specification that occurs much earlier than previously thought (Clements et al., 2011; Kobayashi et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Zangptls exert their effects on definitive hematopoiesis during vascular specifications of the axial vessels including the DA.
source: Based on our genetic data in zebrafish in which we observed a tight genetic interaction between zangptls and notch (Figure 2), we believe that zangptls exert their effects on definitive hematopoiesis during the vascular specifications of the axial vessels including the DA, when it coincides with the highest endogenous expression of zangptl2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inference based on genetic interaction data and expression pattern.

claim: DeltaC has considerable overlapping expression both spatially and temporally with notch in the developing DA.
source: One of the notch ligands, deltaC, has considerable overlapping expression both spatially and temporally with notch in the developing DA, suggesting that it may play a role during the formation of the hemogenic endothelium and the subsequent generation of HSPCs.
evidence: Statement about expression pattern with inference about potential role.

claim: DeltaC expression, normally absent in the DA of mib, was rescued in Tg(hsp70:zangptl2);mib.
source: DeltaC expression, normally absent in the DA of mib was similarly rescued in Tg(hsp70:zangptl2);mib (data not shown).
evidence: Statement about unpublished data.

claim: The relationship between NOTCH and MYC has been best studied in T-ALL cells.
source: The relationship between NOTCH and MYC has been best studied in T-ALL cells whereby MYC transduces growth and survival signals to many NOTCH-dependent T-ALL cell lines and forced ectopic expression of MYC can restore the leukemogenic signals for these cells in instances when NOTCH is inhibited (Palomero et al., 2006; Weng et al., 2006; Chan et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Myc has not been studied in zebrafish hematopoiesis prior to this study.
source: However, myc has not been studied in zebrafish hematopoiesis.
evidence: Statement of novelty based on literature knowledge.

claim: GSEA comparing ANGPTL2-induced gene expression signature to MYC target genes bound by NOTCH from ChIP-seq data found significant overlap.
source: Furthermore, we ran GSEA comparing our ANGPTL2-induced gene expression signature to the set of MYC target genes whose regulatory elements were bound by NOTCH from our ChIP-seq data and found significant overlap (Figure 4E).
evidence: GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The set of MYC targets downstream of ANGPTL2 and NOTCH signaling is highly similar.
source: This implies that the set of MYC targets downstream of ANGPTL2 and NOTCH signaling is highly similar, supporting our hypothesis that ANGPTL may signal partially through NOTCH.
evidence: Inference based on GSEA analysis results.

claim: Purified ANGPTL2 ligand added to cells can rapidly induce NOTCH activation.
source: We first discovered that purified ANGPTL2 ligand added to cells can rapidly induce NOTCH activation, measurable using three different assays: a luciferase reporter assay (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), qPCR of known NOTCH target genes (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), and Western blotting for the NOTCH cleavage product NICD (Figure 5A).
evidence: Summary of multiple experimental approaches demonstrating ANGPTL2-induced NOTCH activation.

claim: ANGPTL2-stimulated S2 cleavage of NOTCH occurs at the cell surface when NOTCH engages with its ligands.
source: Of particular note, when we used different drugs that block certain cleavage events, we found that ANGPTL2-stimulated S2 cleavage of NOTCH (Figure 5C). Interestingly, this step occurs at the cell surface when NOTCH engages with its ligands.
evidence: Statement combining experimental observation with established knowledge about NOTCH cleavage.

claim: ANGPTL2 can induce NOTCH receptor cleavage/activation occurring at the level of ANGPTL receptor binding to NOTCH.
source: Together our data provide insight to the angptl-mediated notch activation through receptor interaction and subsequent activation of myc targets.
evidence: Summary statement from the abstract based on all experimental data.

claim: NOTCH receptors oligomerize at the cell surface at sites of DSL ligand contact from neighboring cells.
source: Indeed several studies have suggested that Notch receptors oligomerize at the cell surface at sites of DSL ligand contact from neighboring cells (Luty et al., 2007; Nichols et al., 2007).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Various alternative non-DSL type ligands have been identified to activate NOTCH.
source: Various alternative non-DSL type ligands have been identified to activate NOTCH, such as the adhesion molecule F3/Contactin (Hu et al., 2003), EGF-repeat factor DNER (Eiraku et al., 2005), EGF-like domain 7 (Schmidt et al., 2009), and Microfibrillar associated glycoproteins (MAGP) 1 and 2 (Miyamoto et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published literature.

evidence: Clarification statement about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: Delta1ext−IgG-expanded HSPCs showed great clinical promise in rapid hematopoietic engraftment with shortened time to neutrophil recovery.
source: More recently, Delta1ext−IgG-expanded HSPCs showed great clinical promise in rapid hematopoietic engraftment with shortened time to neutrophil recovery (Delaney et al., 2010).

source: Furthermore, these expansions were effectively abrogated when cells were treated with a combination of NOTCH1 and NOTCH2 blocking antibodies, suggesting that they were at least partially NOTCH mediated.

claim: ANGPTLs and NOTCH can interact in human cord blood CD34+ cells.
source: This supports that the ANGPTLs and NOTCH can interact in another cell type such as human cord blood CD34+ cells.

claim: HSPCs in zebrafish arise from specialized kdrl-positive hemogenic endothelial cells in the dorsal aorta.
